lead: Air inside a cylinder is never still. Inlet ports, the piston and the chamber shape set up large, organised rotations: swirl about the cylinder axis, squish as the piston pushes gas inward near top dead centre, and tumble about a diameter. These motions break up fuel, carry it through the charge and raise flame speed. They matter in diesel (CI) engines for fuel-air mixing and in petrol (SI) engines for fast, stable combustion. The swirl ratio compares swirl speed with engine speed.
prereq: You need: engine components from Unit 1, and CI mixture formation from Chapter 3.5.

blocks.text: Air motion is the organised movement of the charge inside the cylinder. Inlet ports, valve masks and chamber shape start it during intake; the rising piston changes it near TDC. The three named patterns are:

items: Swirl: bulk rotation about the cylinder axis.
Squish: radial inward flow from the clearance space as the piston nears top dead centre (TDC). Some syllabi call it squish flow.
Tumble: bulk rotation about a diameter of the cylinder, so the charge rolls like a wheel.

blocks.text: These motions are not random turbulence. They are large-scale rotations with a clear direction. As they decay, they break into turbulence: small, random eddies that mix fuel and air at the smallest scale. Organised motion and turbulence are linked, but not the same. The purpose is practical. In a diesel (CI) engine, air motion must reach the injected fuel and mix it with air. In a petrol (SI) engine, air motion must wrinkle the flame front and carry the flame through the charge quickly. Without organised motion, mixing is slow and combustion is uneven.
Swirl is rotation of the whole charge about the cylinder axis. A directed inlet port, a helical port or a masked valve can create it. The swirl ratio compares swirl speed with engine speed:

blocks.where: R<sub>s</sub> is swirl ratio (no units); N<sub>swirl</sub> is swirl speed in rpm; N<sub>engine</sub> is engine speed in rpm. The rpm units cancel, so the ratio has no units.

blocks.text: A ratio of 2.2 means the charge turns 2.2 times for each engine revolution. In a CI engine, swirl carries the fuel spray around the chamber. Fuel that leaves the nozzle into moving air meets fresh oxygen sooner. This shortens the mixing-controlled burn and reduces smoke. In an SI engine, swirl can raise flame speed by increasing turbulence near the spark plug. Too much swirl can increase heat loss to the walls and pump loss. The right amount depends on chamber shape and speed. See Chapter 3.8 for chamber designs that use swirl.

sections.h3: Squish, tumble and the link to combustion

blocks.text: Squish is the radial inward flow that appears as the piston nears TDC. The squish area is the flat part of the piston crown or head outside the bowl. The squish clearance is the gap between piston and head at TDC. As the piston rises, gas in that gap is pushed inward into the bowl or central chamber. The flow is strongest near TDC, when the clearance is smallest.

Squish helps in two ways. In a CI engine it disturbs the fuel spray and pushes air into the bowl, so fuel and air mix faster. In an SI engine it adds turbulence near TDC, which raises flame speed and shortens combustion. Some syllabi call squish flow by that name.

Tumble is rotation about a diameter. The charge rolls from the intake side to the exhaust side. Tumble is common in SI engines with upright intake ports. It stores motion during intake and releases it as turbulence near TDC. That turbulence raises flame speed, so the engine can run lean or with more exhaust gas recirculation.

All three motions feed turbulence. Turbulence increases the area of the flame front and the contact between fuel and air. The result is faster combustion and less cycle-to-cycle variation. See Chapter 3.2 for flame speed and pressure rise.

examples.question: A four-stroke engine runs at 2000 rpm. Its swirl ratio is 2.2. The squish clearance is 2 mm and the average squish velocity is 10 m/s. Find the swirl speed in rpm and the time for the squish flow to move 2 mm. Give the time in milliseconds.
steps: Swirl ratio definition: R<sub>s</sub> = N<sub>swirl</sub> / N<sub>engine</sub>, so N<sub>swirl</sub> = R<sub>s</sub> × N<sub>engine</sub>.
Average velocity: v = 10 m/s. Time t = s / v = 0.002 m / 10 m/s = 0.0002 s.
Convert to milliseconds: t = 0.0002 s × 1000 ms/s = 0.2 ms.
examples.answer: The swirl speed is 4400 rpm and the squish flow takes 0.2 ms to move 2 mm.
examples.check:
engine_rpm = 2000
swirl_ratio = 2.2
swirl_speed = swirl_ratio * engine_rpm
print(swirl_speed)
clearance_mm = 2
velocity_m_s = 10
clearance_m = clearance_mm / 1000
time_s = clearance_m / velocity_m_s
time_ms = time_s * 1000
print(time_ms)

traps: Swirl ratio is not an angle. It is N<sub>swirl</sub> / N<sub>engine</sub> and has no units.
Squish is radial inward flow as the piston nears TDC. It is not rotation about the cylinder axis.
Swirl and tumble have different axes: swirl about the cylinder axis, tumble about a diameter.
In time calculations, convert mm to m. Mixing mm with m/s is a common unit slip.
Swirl is organised motion. Turbulence is small random eddies. Swirl can create turbulence, but the two terms are not interchangeable.

quiz.a: Swirl is bulk rotation of the charge about the cylinder axis. Tumble is bulk rotation about a diameter of the cylinder.

quiz.q: Write the swirl ratio formula and state its unit.
quiz.a: R<sub>s</sub> = N<sub>swirl</sub> / N<sub>engine</sub>. It has no units.

quiz.q: Why does squish flow become strong near TDC?
quiz.a: The squish clearance becomes small as the piston nears TDC. Gas in that gap is squeezed inward into the bowl or central chamber, so the radial inward velocity rises.

quiz.q: How does swirl help CI mixture formation?
quiz.a: Swirl carries the fuel spray around the chamber. Fuel meets fresh oxygen sooner, so mixing is faster and the mixing-controlled burn is shorter.

quiz.q: An engine runs at 3000 rpm with swirl ratio 1.8. Find the swirl speed in rpm.
The squish clearance is 3 mm and the average squish velocity is 12 m/s. Find the time to move 3 mm in milliseconds.
Two engines run at the same speed. One has swirl ratio 3.0 and the other 1.5. Discuss the likely effect on mixing and heat loss.
quiz.a: The higher-swirl engine mixes fuel and air faster and shortens the mixing-controlled burn. It also has more wall contact and pumping loss, so heat loss is higher. The lower-swirl engine mixes more slowly but loses less heat. The best value balances smoke and efficiency.

quiz.q: Why can too much tumble hurt an SI engine?
quiz.a: Too much tumble raises turbulence and burn rate, but it also increases heat transfer to the walls and flow loss. The engine can lose efficiency even though combustion is fast. The chamber and port must be matched to the speed range.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production engine developers use computational fluid dynamics to shape ports and piston bowls before cutting metal. Optical engines and laser diagnostics show swirl, squish and tumble inside a running cylinder; see Unit 6. Variable valve timing and variable geometry turbochargers change air motion across the speed range; see Unit 4. Search terms: swirl ratio, squish velocity, tumble ratio, in-cylinder flow PIV.
